kurz: When pure sugar gets very hot, it breaks down into hundreds of new compounds: brown colour, caramel aroma and in the end bitterness.
bild_im_kopf: Like a sunset in the pan: from colourless through gold and amber to dark brown. Shortly after, night falls, and it turns bitter.
was_passiert: Unlike the [[maillard-reaktion|Maillard reaction]], caramelisation needs no protein, only [[zucker|sugar]] and high heat. Table sugar starts to caramelise at roughly 160 °C. The darker it gets, the less sweet and the more bitter.
warum_wichtig: Gives [[g-creme-brulee|crème brûlée]], caramel sauce, candied almonds and roasted [[zwiebel|onions]] their depth. It almost always runs alongside the Maillard reaction.
faustregeln: Use a pan with a light-coloured base so you can see the colour.
Do not stir; swirl instead, otherwise the sugar crystallises.
Amber is usually ideal. A splash of cold water or cream stops the browning.

praxis.text: Caramel sauce: melt sugar to amber, then stir in warm cream and butter.
With onions and carrots, caramelisation and Maillard run together.
